question_text: A 17-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a severe headache. The patient has had headaches in the past, but she describes this as the worst headache of her life. Her symptoms started yesterday and have been getting progressively worse. The patient states that the pain is mostly on one side of her head. There has been a recent outbreak of measles at the patient’s school, and the patient’s mother has been trying to give her daughter medicine to prevent her from getting sick, but the mother fears that her daughter may have caught the measles. On physical exam, you note an obese young girl who is clutching her head with the light in the room turned off. Her neurological exam is within normal limits. Fundoscopic exam reveals mild bilateral papilledema. A MRI of the head is obtained and reveals cerebral edema. A lumbar puncture reveals an increased opening pressure with a normal glucose level. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

                    ### Question
                    A 17-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a severe headache. The patient has had headaches in the past, but she describes this as the worst headache of her life. Her symptoms started yesterday and have been getting progressively worse. The patient states that the pain is mostly on one side of her head. There has been a recent outbreak of measles at the patient’s school, and the patient’s mother has been trying to give her daughter medicine to prevent her from getting sick, but the mother fears that her daughter may have caught the measles. On physical exam, you note an obese young girl who is clutching her head with the light in the room turned off. Her neurological exam is within normal limits. Fundoscopic exam reveals mild bilateral papilledema. A MRI of the head is obtained and reveals cerebral edema. A lumbar puncture reveals an increased opening pressure with a normal glucose level. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Viral meningitis
opb. Bacterial meningitis
opc. Subarachnoid hemorrhage
opd. Migraine headache
ope. Fat-soluble vitamin overuse

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's presentation includes a severe headache described as the worst of her life, unilateral pain, light sensitivity, normal neurological exam, mild bilateral papilledema, cerebral edema on MRI, increased opening pressure on lumbar puncture, and normal glucose level in CSF. These findings are most consistent with idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), often associated with obesity and potentially linked to fat-soluble vitamin overuse, particularly vitamin A. The presence of papilledema and increased opening pressure without infection or hemorrhage supports this diagnosis. Viral and bacterial meningitis typically present with abnormal CSF glucose levels and more pronounced neurological symptoms. Subarachnoid hemorrhage would likely show blood in the CSF. Migraine headaches do not typically cause papilledema or increased CSF pressure. Therefore, the most likely diagnosis is fat-soluble vitamin overuse leading to IIH.
